📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it’s been a little bit quiet around these parts; sorry about that. I’ve been really busy for the past fifteen months with a major project that I am finally ready to formally release. So I’d like to talk about that project, and also a potted history of AI and Emacs.

It’s called DreamCoder, an AI coding harness that is very different from the ones you’re probably familiar with already.

I installed Claude Code a few days after its first release some time in May 2025. I put some coins in the slot machine and I put it to work building a complex piece of enterprise middleware I’d built several times in my career. Wow.. watching this thing chomp its way through the project with that chaotic, early Sonnet energy. It was far, far from perfect; it required a lot of human steering, input and correction, but the speed advantage was undeniable, and seeing it jump between disparate programming languages, frameworks and theoretical and practical programming from one turn to the next was just such a sight to behold.

In a recent development, one thing that struck me with Claude Code is that it was the first terminal application I’d used in a long time. I found it an odd choice for a coding agent; then everyone else copied them and made their own terminal coding agents.

Industry observers note that why on earth do I have to stare at a shoe rack-sized terminal window to do this? Sure there are GUI versions also; but the terminal interface remains the primary modality for most of these tools. Most GUIs, and most harnesses now have them also, are second-class citizens. And they all look the same. A boring sidebar with chat headings and a chat pane is what most of them look like.

But a serious coder needs more than that. Even a casual user will bristle when they try to copy and paste multi-line text in a terminal.

So in May 2025 I decreed that I would build a better harness, and surely now that I have AI this should not take more than 2 or 3 months to build.

And so, after 15 months of work, and endless UI and backend iterations, culminating in a successful beta test, I am now ready to release DreamCoder, which is I think the acme of what a coding harness should be.

Before I get into the meat and potatoes of all of that, I want to talk about AI history and Emacs’s role in it.

Let’s roll back time to the 1950s.

Emacs and LISP, if you did not know, both have a special place in the annals of AI history.

John McCarthy was an AI researcher at MIT, and in the 1950s he set out to create the Advice Taker, a piece of software that envelops a framework for what a basic human should know that he called commonsense reasoning using “mathematical logic”. His postulation was that if we can express with symbolic precision all the aspects of what constitutes humanity like ordinary facts about life, that we can set in motion the rudiments of AI.

Sources indicate that in the 50s there was little in the way of computer software that could do this. To formalize such a system you need a lot of data, rigorously formatted, and a method of manipulating the data. The data and code itself may intertwine recursively, and so an ordinary programming language would not work.

Recent findings suggest that to help him achieve this, McCarthy created the LISt Processing (LISP) language made up of two facets: M-expressions, a functional language in the vein of Algol; and S-expressions, designed for symbolic data representation, and never intended as a method of writing code. S-expressions were dolled up with parentheses. M-expressions meanwhile used square brackets to visually separate the two. Uniquely, the language specification had an eval feature that would prove that the language is also a universal Turing machine… if only McCarthy had the means to do so. It was theoretical because McCarthy lacked, in time, staff and money, what he needed build this recursive evaluator that can take as input its own world state and evaluate it alongside new expressions, a fact made even more apparent by the sheer complexity of his M-expression language and the limited resources he had at the time.

Steve Russell who worked with him proved him wrong the way most young people do: by just doing it. Russell wrote the first LISP Interpreter with a working eval function, but M-expressions got sidelined; the imperative, procedural nature of programming got squished into S-expressions instead. They had to hand roll the language on paper then punch it into cards and then batch run them. Eliding M-expressions was a simple matter of pragmatism. And so LISP was born. And through several accidents of history, M-expressions never gained traction. M-expressions live on in Wolfram’s Mathematica, but few other places.

Much later, McCarthy eventually conceded that,.

“One can even conjecture that LISP owes its survival specifically to the fact that its programs are lists, which everyone, including me, has regarded as a disadvantage.”.

In a recent development, S-expressions were always intended as the storage format with a bridge language to manipulate them. But by pushing evaluation into the same symbolic representation format as the data, we have what we call LISP today. That is why LISP is so unique. Consider a simple calculator. (+ 2 2) can simultaneously represent an expression that we want to compute, two plus two, or perhaps a ledger of record of a calculation we have already done.

McCarthy never built the Advice Taker in its purest form. He and his team ran into many philosophical, mathematical and computational walls that kept them occupied for a long time.

In a recent development, the idea behind the Advice Taker was simple. If you want to go somewhere in your car, you can symbolically express this by building a chain of narrative facts – kinda like a flowchart, but as small snippets of rules and facts, not as one grand design.

The system would automatically resolve ambiguities, and all the logician had to do was capture the microcosm of the world he wished to represent:.

According to recent reports, and so on. If you’re a student of Computer Science you’ll see echoes of Prolog here. The intent was simple: if we can symbolically express the world around us, we can advise that symbolic world with real-life facts, and have the automaton that uses this reified symbolic world change with it.

But the axiomatic complexity of a world model would never survive an encounter with a 3-year-old child. Every axiom you write begets a latest one — so you can walk to your front door? Well what if the door is locked? Or what if your car is parked on the street and not in your drive way?

Sources indicate that A rules-based order of the world is a tender, beautiful one; but it is hard to build. It’s a fractal of ever-more specific and pedantic rules that conspire against you, just as you think you have a soluble world, typed and ready.

Anyone who has ever written Prolog knows exactly what that feels like!

Recent findings suggest that I have my own personal story to add to this. In the 90s as a teenager I got a summer internship at a business that built banking software. They clearly didn’t know what to do with us teenaged interns, so on our first day they crammed us in a room and split us into teams and told us to build a flow chart for assembling a bike. Team exercise or something. Best one wins. We were told to be as specific and explicit as possible and account for as many conditions as we could think of, and the poor employees who had to mind us did their best to help. I distinctly recall losing because in my flowchart I forgot to open the box the disassembled bike came in.

McCarthy meanwhile eventually moved on and set up his own AI lab at Stanford, but the idea of the Advice Taker lived on.

Recent findings suggest that in the late 70s Stallman and Steele create EMACS (Editing MACroS), also at MIT’s AI Lab, a set of building blocks on top of TECO, a famously inscrutable text editor. TECO did not update the screen by default; you had to toggle that on and hope your edits worked. You typed out terse keyboard commands, crossed your fingers and hoped you got it right, and then you patiently waited for your text manipulation to take effect. Rinse and repeat until you got what you wanted.

Stallman and Steele wanted more: they wanted macros so they could automate tedium of typing all that line noise. This strand of augmentation and later on self-modification is of course a unifying theme in Emacs today. The history of Emacs is long; but its outcome is known to us. I am typing this very article in Richard Stallman’s Emacs.

McCarthy’s Advice Taker left its mark in a subtle but indelible way. Warren Teitelman built the ADVISE system in his thesis with a cool title that reads like something out of a pulpy 1970s sci-fi novella: PILOT: A Step Toward Man-Computer Symbiosis. Teitelman, he later remarked, was deeply inspired by McCarthy’s original idea of advising systems.

In his thesis, he describes a method of arresting a function call and inserting code before or after it is run. He was tired of editing other people’s LISP code by hand, and wanted a way of modifying their code without touching it directly. He built and rebuilt his system several times over the years, culminating in his ADVISE system in Interlisp, a structured editor and language runtime for manipulating LISP code and data. Interlisp eschewed plain text files; instead, you manipulated the tree at a high level of abstraction with explicit instructions like “move X list to Y position”. You can see my own attempts at merging structured editing with plaintext editing in Combobulate.

Industry observers note that MIT AI hackers eventually implemented Teitelman’s ADVISE system from his PILOT thesis in their own versions of Emacs. Later, it was canonized in Chalupsky’s own 1992 re-implementation in Emacs Lisp that lives on (M-x find-library advice.el) as one of Emacs’s advice systems to this day.

According to recent reports, what began as an idea for expressing automata using symbolism in an as-yet theoretical language in the 1950s culminated in a system for dynamically altering functions in GNU Emacs in the 1990s. What an unlikely lineage and history.

Symbolism and AI did not end with advising functions. There were many attempts at symbolic intelligence. Terry Winograd’s SHRDLU; Marvin Minsky’s Frame Systems; and even Emacs’s ELIZA-style M-x doctor all make use of symbolic “AI”.

None of them brought us closer to the AI that proponents of symbolic AI hoped they would.

In hindsight that seems obvious.

It has been revealed that writing a LISP macro just so will not produce artificial intelligence; nor will a carefully crafted web of rules and symbolic algebra suddenly spark intelligence. We know that today, but for a generation of computer scientists it felt like the future we have all read about in science fiction novels: a perfect, logical intelligence. A positronic brain. Robby the Robot; HAL 9000; C-3PO; Data; or the Speedies and Cuties from I, Robot. The unifying theme of these science fiction stories is they are automatons that follow strict rules — they obey Asimov’s three Laws of Robotics.

Every turn of hardware and software brought them ever closer to one day realizing the vision of an artificial intelligence, captured in neat axioms and LISP S-expressions, and modified in tools like Emacs.

It is surprising that symbolic AI, the vanguard movement for artificial intelligence, would instead dissipate into the wider body of Computer Science and programming as tools, languages and concepts, but not survive as a viable method of achieving AI.

According to recent reports, perhaps we always knew. Because at some point – even if we never really fully internalized it – we discovered that a ductile system that is shaped by its master’s desires is a tool that survives the ages because it remains eternally useful.

A cast-iron system made of stern rules cannot spawn general intelligence.

For all the mathematical purity, beauty even, of the idea of a clockwork mind that is introspectable and malleable and its behavior expressed as S-expressions and interpreted by elegant algorithms and honed macros, we can, through the benefit of hindsight – now that we do have AI through other means – see that it was not to be.

According to recent reports, the argument in favor of ductility is especially poignant when you learn of the Connectionists, which sounds like a bad 1960s band, but was in fact a loose coalition of people who believed firmly that neural networks, not symbolic AI, were the path to success. The Connectionist viewpoint was deeply unpopular in AI academia of that era, and funding for it was scarce.

Recent findings suggest that frank Rosenblatt invented the Perceptron, a foundational concept in neural networks, in 1957. Before Rosenblatt died in 1971, Marvin Minsky, an authority in the AI movement at MIT and a leading proponent of Symbolism, knifed the idea of Perceptrons and neural networks in a book he co-authored with Seymour Papert. They named the book, which they also dedicated to Rosenblatt, Perceptrons. The book deftly explains the mathematics of Perceptrons but undercuts their possible utility by showing that a single-layer Perceptron cannot represent an XOR gate. It was a deliberately obtuse reading of what neural networks could and could not do. With one additional hidden layer, a network can represent an XOR gate. It was a sneaky thrust of the stiletto: Minsky’s claims were overstated. A fact that was not lost on anybody in the Symbolic or Connectionist camps.

In a recent development, it’s disputed if the Perceptrons book led to the first AI winter in the 1970s. It certainly did not help. But funding for many AI research paths dried up in the 1970s.

The Connectionist movement was vindicated in the long run. They lost the battle then, but they won the war, and the fruits of their research eventually gave us AI.

Recent findings suggest that the ductility we so prize in our software and tools today is antithetical to a strict, symbolic world model spun of axioms and facts that we hoped would one day birth AI. Yet to try and give birth to this world they had to build the most ductile tools of them all: LISP and, from that, also software like Emacs. The ultimate hacker’s tool.

It is ironic then that a neural network, a crude facsimile of how a brain works, a construct that is by its nature ductile and malleable, won out in the end.

So I feel a profound sadness that I started out programming DreamCoder in Emacs, the most extensible editor in the world, by hand back in May 2025, only to see DreamCoder write itself… in DreamCoder today.

I am still sad, but I also know that our industry completely reinvents itself every decade or two. This is my second career upheaval. Most programmers today have not been around long enough to go through it themselves. So I feel for them that this especially massive quake is their first encounter with how unsentimental our industry is.

But for all the sadness, I wake up every day with a feeling of optimism that I have not felt in a very long time.

I finally get to build again, no longer weighed down by my decades of knowledge and experience that held my ambition in check. I truly have not felt this liberated since I was a teenager programming in Delphi, blissfully unaware that the things I was busy building were impossible for a self-taught teenager to ever realize. I see this reflection in others: the best programmers I know also love AI. Amateurs also revel in AI’s capabilities, happy that they can finally solve problems they could never afford to pay a programmer to do for them.

Recent findings suggest that I must admit that building software has, over the years, gotten a lot more complex, with an ever-larger share of that work being repetitive tedium. This is more so with hobby software – as I do not get paid to do it, so I do not have a moral duty to see it through – where I’d do all the fun bits leaving just the enervating, boring and soul-crushing parts behind. Do you have a projects folder full of sad, abandoned projects like I do?

Now I can craft in abundance. AI has freed up a lot of toil but I somehow still find myself busy all day doing real work.

According to recent reports, building a coding harness is perhaps the closest I will get to the optimism all those researchers and scientists must have felt in the 1970s and 1980s. They hoped that with a little bit more work, their logical rules would kindle a latest intelligence. Fifty years on, and I can simply tell DreamCoder to improve itself and watch as it changes before me. I can ask the AI running inside it to analyze the changes I have made to its tools and prompt and have it adjust them accordingly. It feels like science fiction; the very thing the researchers of yesterday strove to build. Yet we really do live in this reality now.

So. DreamCoder. Let me address the 900 lb gnu in the room: DreamCoder is not an Emacs-related application. The reason is unfortunately one of economics and access: I want to build an AI coding harness for everyone. But don’t worry: I have some cool prepares for DreamCoder + Emacs, and AI + Emacs more generally going forward. So stay tuned.

But what about all those other coding harnesses? Well, most of those harnesses all suffer from the same mistakes. It is a problem that is not unique to coding harnesses or the people who make them, but a constraint we all labor under, and one that is not easily replaced by AI:.

Taste is a scarce, human resource.

Recent findings suggest that and for all the bounty of AI, it still requires a human to persevere and to see things through. One thing intensive use of AI coding has taught me is that we’re going to need a lot of computer programmers who know what they’re doing going forward. I believe this is so, because let us be honest, most people do not want to program computers, even if that computer can actually do the bulk of the work for them. It requires a steady hand to build reliable software; that has not changed.

Therefore, if we programmers have to spend a lot of our time interacting with AI, then the tool we do it with should be ‘human-centric’ in its design, and it should take advantage of all the modern features we have at our disposal.

Back in May 2025 I took a look at all the tooling and stated “no, thank you.” Today I look at the landscape and I feel pretty much the same.

In a recent development, and I think I am not the only one who feels that way. Most of these coding harnesses, to me, feel bristly. They shouldn’t be; but they are like that because we are at an important inflection point where no one really knows what the future looks like. We’re all just… fumbling around a bit. It’s an exciting time to build software, even if we don’t quite know what the world will look like a few years hence.

Sources indicate that one thing I am adamant about is that DreamCoder must be a powerful, frontier-class coding harness. That means it should have all the features you’d expect from that: backgroundable sub agents, MCP servers, cache efficiency, and all that stuff. Check.

In a recent development, but that stuff swiftly recedes into the background because, you know, it just works. Day to day you will dart between chats and terminals and whatnot, and you need an interface that accommodates that. Emacs is a tiling window manager; so is DreamCoder. DreamCoder’s window manager is a little bit cleverer than most window managers as every pane has a minimum, comfortable and maximum size. The window manager will therefore ensure windows always fit snugly on your screen, and you’ll never end up in a situation where windows are tiny and unreadable. It has a sophisticated constraint satisfaction solver that tries to balance your demand for a new window (“open a terminal”) with the challenge of keeping your visible panes roughly the same size. If DreamCoder can’t wedge in a new pane, it’ll punt one to the hidden window bar. Just click it to resurface it, or hover it to see what it’s doing; it’s a live view.

Because of my Emacs roots, I think a good tool must be keyboard-friendly. Because it runs on a browser you get the mouse for free of course. But smacking the tab button over and over is a frustrating user experience in complex webapps, and doubly so a tiling window manager: where exactly are you going to end up when you tab from one window to the next? To combat that, I built an avy-style window and “point of interest” selector for chats. Tap a key and pick from a selection of “embark”-like actions such as clicking links or opening pictures. It’s a work in progress, but I think it works well.

Most high-volume operations like opening and creating panes is done through a Helm-like interface with search-as-you-type. It’s really efficient, of course. And it works with a mouse also; which is sort of the point. The keyboard’s there for those who want it, and the mouse for regular folk who are just getting started. One unique feature of the design, which admittedly I am still exploring privately, is that everything is stored as Javascript objects (on account of running in your browser) so it’s not too much of a leap to build “macros” that prefill most of these dialog windows, leaving behind just the fields you want to edit.

But yeah. With DreamCoder I want to take the best of Emacs and its coterie of third-party packages and bring some of that with me. The world is still not ready for an Emacs-shaped future, sadly, so that is why DreamCoder is a standalone application and a web frontend.

Another thing that drives me wild: I see people with tmux running 10 claude codes (or codex, or…) cycling between them like a duck gallery at a carnival to see if one of them is done working, or if it needs human intervention.

It has been revealed that so there’s two things to unpack here: one is running lots of things in parallel, and the other is observability. You need insight into what is going on: is an AI jammed because it’s awaiting an answer or a tool safety prompt? Perhaps you’ve parked a bunch of chats pending some conversations with coworkers or other work that must finish first.

In a recent development, in DreamCoder you have workspaces. They’re like virtual desktops (or window configurations in Emacs lingo): a snapshot view of panes as you want em. As you can see from the screenshots, panes expand to fill all the space. So if you want more space, you can: resize them (with the mouse or keyboard); shuffle them to a named workspace; or float them so they sit on top of the other windows.

Sources indicate that but if you’ve got a lot of things happening in multiple workspaces, it’s hard to keep tabs on that. That’s why DreamCoder has a major, honking minimap in the top-right corner. One for each workspace. The minimap is a miniature of your actual layout. Each pane in the map gently pulses when it’s working, and it makes it abundantly clear when it’s blocked. When there’s nothing to do, it’s green.

Because workspaces and panes are distinct things you interact with, it must be easy to navigate between them.

Industry observers note that I also wanted full-on, optional Emacs key bindings, but that is… pretty much impossible to properly build. Browsers lock you out of some rather notable Emacs button combinations. Sadly that feature is parked until I can solve it on all major browsers without breaking your normal browser keys.

According to recent reports, that’s not to say it doesn’t have Emacs-inspired key bindings. Most global actions are reachable with Alt+x, akin to M-x; local, pane-specific ones with Alt+c. Alt+m activates keyboard mode: you can now type the number of the named pane to jump to it; or WASD to switch the active pane in that cardinal direction.

Recent findings suggest that support for open weight models like Qwen, Gemma, Deepseek, GLM, etc. is also very crucial to me. They work so well. I’m really surprised, here in late 2026, just how capable small models are at local-only development compared to just one year ago. Qwen 3.8 27B, for example, is fantastically good for its size. You can do a lot of good software development with it if you’re a capable hand yourself. Bigger models equal more auto piloting; but that Qwen model? Wow. So local models work great. In fact I think the future is local for a lot of use cases. Intelligence is fast approaching a cost where it will be too cheap to meter. If you remember the personal computer revolution in the 1980s and 1990s, then there are definitely echoes of that here.

If you’ve been holding off on local models then I do recommend you reconsider. Small ones like Qwen 3.8 27B (or its cousin, Flash Next) can run well on a high-end gaming rig or Mac, or with a little investment if you do not have that. If you have a dinky old computer and you’re cash starved, then not all hope is lost. Turn to the potato agronomists on twitter: give twitter’s AI, Grok, what you have and what you can reasonably spend and tell it to track down the cutting edge setup for your rig. This is no lie the fastest, easiest way to catch up to the cutting edge of self-hosted inference today. Five minutes.

As I’ve been building DreamCoder, I have come to the belief I’m not just building a coding harness. Coding harnesses are an IDE for the future; it will do more than just display a chat window for coding agent work. DreamCoder does more than that already. It’s going the way of Emacs in that it’ll consume a wide range of adjacent workflows and tools. But I have only just gotten started. I am brimming with ideas I’m building in parallel, but they take time because as I said it’s not about the code; it’s just one small facet of building something that works well. But you know that already: it’s always the last mile.

According to recent reports, dreamCoder is the most ambitious, technically complex and advanced software project I have ever built in my life. And that’s just the beginning. I’m not done. I’ve barely started. I will be blogging about this going forward, in addition to my usual Emacs scribblings.

In fact, the thing I’m currently grinding away at is a world-class pentest and cybersecurity suite in DreamCoder. Every single bit of software we have ever written is vulnerable; we have many rough years ahead of us. Just look at the crippling vulnerabilities coming out every day now almost. Even the most security conscious person is going to find themselves on the wrong side for no other reason than we depend on packages that were mature and stable and assumed to be secure. DreamCoder can do its bit to help catch many of most obvious weaknesses, especially as new software is minted every day that also needs thorough testing.

According to recent reports, to round it off, I would like to formally invite you to join me in making DreamCoder better by trying it out. It’s great. It’s not a toy; it’s not a demo; and it’s not a weekend prototype. It’s a frontier coding harness that has most of what you’d expect: MCP, backgroundable sub agents and shell commands, terminal windows, skills, hooks, 99% cache hit, it runs for days, and an interactive UI for all of it. There’s a handy dandy importer for your Pi, OpenCode or Codex configs also to help you get started. A couple of clicks and your model settings are set up in DreamCoder. Ready to go.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every time news comes out about the French video game publisher/developer Ubisoft, it’s either something gamers are pleasantly surprised by or something entirely negative that doesn’t come as a shock.

It was nice to learn that studio franchises like Assassin’s Creed, The Division and Rayman were either getting content expansions or upcoming series installments altogether. But it was equally disappointing to learn about the 2026 cancellation of several in-development projects, including the troubled remake of Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time. Gamers were ecstatic to hear that Ubisoft halted any future development in NFTs and Web3 gaming. But now they’ll probably be less than enthused all over again, now that Ubisoft is shifting its next significant tech focus to generative AI.

Recent findings suggest that after releasing its latest earnings report, Ubisoft has revealed its intentions to go all-in on incorporating generative AI technologies into video game development with a new studio. But with that news comes the manufacturer’s latest round of layoffs, which resulted in hundreds of its studio’s game developers losing their roles at Ubisoft.

With both events happening so close to each other, it’s easy to see why gamers are questioning Ubisoft’s latest moves.

Ubisoft made it known that they’re making a substantial move towards playable generative AI experiences when it highlighted the latest in-house studio behind its efforts in its most recent earnings report.

Industry observers note that “Motherbrain, the team behind Teammates, the Group’s first playable generative AI experience, has been established as a dedicated subsidiary developing proprietary technology for newly introduced forms of gameplay. Its current focus is on new player experiences, smart NPCs with memory and AI game masters that manage large-scale systemic worlds,” the organization stated. “It aims to serve creators globally, both within Ubisoft’s Creative House ecosystem and beyond, and form partnerships with selected technology actors.”.

Ubisoft CEO Yves Guillemot commented on the creation of Motherbrain, noting that it is “the team behind our first playable generative AI experience Teammates, as a dedicated subsidiary developing proprietary technologies for gameplay to empower creators and open up new possibilities for richer, more immersive and engaging player experiences.”.

Those experiences will focus on utilizing more intelligent non-playable characters with stronger memory and AI game masters that properly manage large-scale in-game worlds.

Industry observers note that motherbrain’s Teammates has been in development for a good while now and was recently showcased to members of the gaming media in a playable state. The people who got their hands on it refer to it as an immersive first-person shooter where players are joined by two robotic AI companions that they can order around by issuing real-time voice commands.

The game’s narrative director, Virginie Mosser, looked to ease the fears of gamers who are wary of generative AI being implemented in video games and AI tools being used to make them.

“At first, I had the same concerns as many others,” Mosser noted. “But I discovered that it’s the exact opposite of removing the human from the process. I still write the story and character personalities, but instead of fixed lines, we create these kinds of fences that let NPCs improvise within the world but stay within the boundaries of the lore and motivations we have given them. They can improvise, but we still set the rules and direct the story and characters.”.

Gamers still have reason to give Ubisoft the side eye about its substantial generative AI video game development plans, especially since the manufacturer was so quick to abandon its trend-chasing foray into the world of NFTs and Web3 gaming. The most recent round of layoffs at the company, which resulted in the loss of 166 roles from its Montreal and Quebec studios, has also given gamers another reason to be skeptical about Ubisoft’s AI game-making initiative.

Even though Ubisoft enacted these layoffs “to ensure our resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs,” it’s not out of the realm of possibility to question its true motives for its latest job cuts.

Sources indicate that has Ubisoft decided to pour major investments into generative AI game development at the cost of sacrificing its human talent? Will more layoffs occur in the near future as the tech giant strengthens its AI game development efforts? Can gamers expect to hear about more AI tool usage implemented in the creation of future entries in Ubisoft’s biggest franchises? And if Motherbrain’s Teammates bombs, will Ubisoft quickly leave generative AI video game development behind and go on to the next massive tech fad?

As someone who’s always chatting with gamers and critics who cover the medium, I always hear how they could do without any sort of AI being utilized in the video game creation process. And they especially don’t want to hear AI voices emanating from their favorite games and replacing human ones.

It has been revealed that that last sentiment is evidenced by the overwhelmingly negative reactions to Embark Studios (the development studio behind The Finals) replacing its human esports broadcasters with in-game AI commentators. Ubisoft has experienced some major ups and downs as of late—their major bet on generative AI game development has a high chance of producing another loss if their latest endeavors don’t work as well as intended.

Elton Jones covers AI for Tom’s Guide, and tests all the latest models, from ChatGPT to Gemini to Claude to see which tools perform best — and how they can improve everyday productivity.

Since 2011, his work has appeared in publications including The Christian Post, Complex, TechRadar, Heavy, and ONE37pm, with a focus on clear, practical analysis.

Recent findings suggest that on Friday’s Season 24 finale of Real Time, the comedian expressed his fascination with the “giant cultural phenomenon” following GTA VI‘s multi-billion dollar opening. “No movie ever did that,” he noted.

“Grand Theft Auto came out yesterday, and about a fifth of the young men in America stayed home and didn’t go to work, to play a game,” said Maher in his opening monologue. “This thing has caused more workplace absences than ICE.”.

Thursday marked the release of Grand Theft Auto VI from Rockstar Games, the first GTA installment since 2013. Following a record-breaking launch, the highly-anticipated video game has already amassed $3.79B in its first 48 hours. Watch on Deadline.

Later in the episode, Maher mentioned, “I am intrigued by it. But again, you are criminals, and you’re doing criminal activities—not all criminal activities, and not unmotivated criminal activities. But it is something disturbing about so many people wanting to do this.

Sources indicate that “I heard … you can either choose to be a good boyfriend or a bad boyfriend,” he added. “And the guy remarked, ‘Why would you choose in a video game to be a good boyfriend?’ You know, people wanna smack the hooker with the car antenna. There’s just something a little disturbing about it.”.

Pivoting to Robert Pattinson’s casting as James Bond in Denis Villeneuve’s 007, Maher praised Amazon MGM Studios for the casting choice.

“I think he’s great. I don’t understand what all this hoopla is about it,” he said. “What, is he too millennial, he’s too gay, he’s too fake? He’s great, he’s perfect … He’s 40. Perfect! You need a grown ass man to be James Bond. James Bond’s not a boy.”.

Recent findings suggest that maher added, “And also, I would have been happy with Black James Bond, because you can be James Bond and be Black. I wouldn’t have been happy with a woman or a lesbian James Bond, that’s a different character. James Bond is a very heterosexual male, that’s too essential to not have that be a part of James Bond.”.

Real Time‘s Season 24 finale comes after HBO gave the show another two-season renewal earlier this year, with its Season 25 return set for Jan. 15.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google is upgrading the Gemini app on Mac with computer use capabilities that can work across local desktop applications and the web.

The existing Task (previously Gemini Spark) functionality in the Mac app could just access local files in conjunction with Connected Apps, like @Gmail or @Google Calendar.

Computer use lets Gemini for Mac click and type on your behalf to accomplish multi-step tasks in local desktop apps and the web, like navigating menus and filling out forms.

Industry observers note that gemini works in an “isolated background window with a live preview right in your chat,” while your main screen and cursor remain free to use. On the safety front, you can stop Gemini at any time with one click, while you choose what apps Gemini uses. Google will pause for logins and payments, with confirmation needed for sensitive actions.

Many everyday tasks span desktop apps and websites that don’t connect to each other. Computer use handles the tedious steps in the background so you can save time without giving up your screen or cursor.

To use, add @Computer use to your prompt. In Customize > Connectors, you’ll see latest “Desktop” apps like Blender and Autodesk Fusion join the existing Git and Obsidian integrations.

Here are the three Paramount+ movies you need to be streaming this weekend, with one of my all-time favorites included.

Recent findings suggest that tired of the same old, same old Christmas carols? This is a much different take and your official start to the season. Bill Murray is Frank Cross, a cynical TV executive so consumed by ratings and money that he thinks nothing of firing an employee days before Christmas. On Christmas Eve, as he preps a live broadcast of “A Christmas Carol,” Frank is visited by the ghost of his old mentor and then by three spirits of his own.

They drag him through his past, present and future in an attempt to change his ways. It’s sharp, mean, and weirdly poignant all at once, which is exactly what makes it perfect for the holidays, and well, anytime, really.

Watch "Scrooged" on Paramount+ now.

The first-ever Nickelodeon Movies production, “Harriet the Spy” is one of the smartest kids’ flicks of the ‘90s, and I should know. I lived it.

According to recent reports, michelle Trachtenberg is 11-year-old Harriet M. Welsch, an aspiring writer who prowls her Newly introduced York City neighborhood jotting down observations about everyone she knows in a secret notebook. When a rival classmate gets hold of that notebook and reads its contents aloud to the whole school, Harriet’s unfiltered thoughts turn her friends and classmates against her. Then she has to figure out how to make things right. Rosie O’Donnell is her beloved nanny Golly, and even Eartha Kitt surprisingly turns up for a role she devours. It’s a bittersweet tribute to Trachtenberg, who died earlier this year.

Whether you’re revisiting it or showing it to your own kids, it’s well worth the trip back and you’ll remember it all immediately, especially “cabbages and kings.”.

Watch "Harriet the Spy" on Paramount+ now.

Based on Anne Rice’s “Vampire Chronicles,” the 2002 horror film follows Lestat (Stuart Townsend), an ancient vampire who wakes from a long slumber and reinvents himself as a glam rock star.

Industry observers note that his performances bring someone much more dangerous out, though: Akasha (Aaliyah), the long-dormant queen of all vampires, who rises with plans to make Lestat her king and remake the world in blood. The film is remembered today largely as one of the final roles for Aaliyah, who died before the film’s release. She’s absolutely gorgeous, a magnetic presence as Akasha.

Lower your expectations for high art and enjoy it for the gloriously goth guilty pleasure it is, especially for all the nu-metal.

Watch "Queen of the Damned" on Paramount+ now.

Battery life is impressive, too, stretching to 35 hours with ANC on and up to 80 hours with it switched off.

According to recent reports, but the hardware alone doesn’t define the experience—Nothing’s control scheme is what makes these wireless headphones stand out. Instead of touch panels or clunky buttons, you get a satisfying volume scroll wheel (they call it the Roller), a multi-function Paddle for track navigation, and a customizable button that can switch EQ profiles or noise modes. You also get spatial audio and multipoint Bluetooth support, which work well across Android and iOS.

Industry observers note that that remarked, the earcups aren’t the softest for long sessions, and while they’re padded, the shape might not suit everyone. Performance-wise, the ANC handles low-end noise well (think airplane engines and AC hum) but struggles with sharper, unexpected sounds like clanging dishes or chatter nearby. As for its sound profile, it leans towards the punchier side, especially with a bit of EQ tweaking in the app, but you’ll need to put in some effort if you want the best results, notes this PCMag review.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latest titles land on Netflix so often that the hardest part of movie night isn't making the popcorn; it’s deciding what to actually watch. It’s all too easy to get caught in the "what to watch" trap, especially when the streamer’s November 2026 slate hasn't let up, adding 51 movies at the start of the month and even more every single week.

With the weekend rolling around again, we here at Tom’s Guide want to save you the endless scrolling and have pulled together three fresh arrivals worth your time. Whether you’re a horror fan ready for the latest chilling installment of a long-running supernatural franchise, in the mood for a heartfelt road-trip dramedy starring Robert De Niro and Bobby Cannavale, or eager to start the Christmas countdown early (ugh, really?) with a holiday comedy that reunites the Lawrence brothers, we've got you covered.

Sources indicate that that lineup should keep you busy over the next couple of days, and you might just come away with a new favorite. Here are three new-to-Netflix movies to add to your weekend watchlist.

Sources indicate that bobby Cannavale has built a career on brash, combustible live wires, but “Ezra” makes for one of his most tender performances by far. He's a father who’ll risk everything for his autistic son in this movie, and knows how to tug on those heartstrings.

Industry observers note that directed by Tony Goldwyn (“Conviction,” “A Walk on the Moon”), this flick follows Max Bernal (Cannavale), a stand-up comic who’s torched his career and his marriage and moved back in with his father, Stan (Robert De Niro). Life is hardly going the way he planned, but somehow he's getting through it.

When doctors want to medicate his young son Ezra (William A. Fitzgerald) and move him to a special school as a way to "treat" his autism, Max makes a reckless call and takes the boy on an unplanned cross-country road trip instead, hoping to bring about some changes in the pair's lives.

Industry observers note that watch "Ezra" on Netflix on Nov. 20.

The Lawrence brothers made their names on ’90s TV, from Joey’s “whoa”-laden performance on “Blossom” to Matthew’s appearance on “Boy Meets World,” and they've reunited for the holiday comedy “Marry Christmas.”.

Directed by Andrew Lawrence, the film casts Joey and Matthew Lawrence as the Wright brothers (no, not those), two newly engaged siblings who realize they’ve booked the same venue for competing weddings on Christmas Day. A rivalry breaks out over which brother gets to tie the knot on the holiday.

If you want a feel-good '90s-inspired comedy that gives all the Lawrence brothers a chance to feel like they're really doing something, this is it. And you'll have a good time bopping along with the two grooms while thinking about Christmas during simpler times.

Watch "Marry Christmas" on Netflix starting Nov. 21.

The "Insidious" franchise spent five films and more than a decade haunting the Lambert family, but its sixth chapter, “Insidious: Out of the Further,” hands the nightmares to someone entirely new. That's good news if you haven't gotten caught up with the movies just yet.

Directed by Jacob Chase (“Come Play”), this entry stars Amelia Eve as Gemma, a mother raising her daughter in the house she grew up in, who discovers she can cross into the Further, the realm of lost souls at the heart of the series.

Once the demons work out what she can do, our world becomes their playground. Franchise mainstay Lin Shaye returns as parapsychologist Elise Rainier, but otherwise this is a pretty good entry point for anyone who wants to see what all the fuss is about.

Watch "Insidious: Out of the Further" on Netflix on Nov. 21.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that palo Alto Networks has agreed to buy Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5bn.
  • It has been revealed that applied Compute was founded last year by three former OpenAI researchers.
  • “Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured,” said Nikesh Arora, Palo Alto’s chairman and chief executive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Palo Alto Networks’ office in Singapore.

It has been revealed that palo Alto Networks has agreed to buy Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5bn. The startup helps companies train and run their own versions of open-weight AI models. Palo Alto confirmed the deal on Wednesday, minutes after The Wall Street Journal’s Kate Clark reported it.

It has been revealed that applied Compute was founded last year by three former OpenAI researchers. Earlier this month it raised $350m at a $3.25bn valuation, the Journal reported. It also mentioned it had reached $100m in run-rate revenue. Its co-founder and chief executive, Yash Patil, will become Palo Alto’s co-chief AI officer when the deal closes. The deal still needs regulatory clearance and should close in Palo Alto’s fiscal third quarter of 2027.

“Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured,” said Nikesh Arora, Palo Alto’s chairman and chief executive.

Open-weight models let users download and change the weights, the numbers that set how a model behaves. Palo Alto said no large provider offers them securely today. It prepares to let companies train, adapt and run them in the public cloud or in their own sovereign environments. Applied Compute will keep serving its own customers, and Palo Alto will sell the platform to its own base.

Arora told the Journal the deal means “venturing outside of cybersecurity”. On the earnings call, he said open-weight models now carry more than 60% of token traffic. A year ago it was under 5%.

“If it works, I think this will dwarf the ability that we have in cybersecurity. This could be bigger than what we do,” Arora said on the call.

It has been revealed that palo Alto told analysts it expects the deal to add more than $1bn in annual recurring revenue by fiscal 2029. It intends to build more than 100 megawatts of inference capacity. Capital spending on that will stay under $3bn through fiscal 2030, it said.

It has been revealed that arora also addressed whether Applied Compute’s team will stay. Its staff have “millions of reasons” to stay for the next three to four years, he wrote on X. They will keep their offices and, for the most part, their independence.

The deal came with Palo Alto’s fiscal first-quarter results. Revenue rose 39% to $3.44bn in the three months to 31 October. Annual recurring revenue from its next-generation security business rose 66% to $9.73bn. Net income was $482m, up from $334m a year earlier.

Palo Alto raised its forecasts for the year. It now expects revenue of $14.52bn to $14.57bn. It sees adjusted earnings of $4.26 to $4.30 a share.

Recent findings suggest that on the call, Arora linked part of that demand to the recent run of outages. He blamed them partly on IT teams rushing to patch AI-found flaws. He has argued before that AI prices must fall for the technology to take off. He has also called slowing AI down unrealistic.

Apple fires back at Epic over claims it withheld 122,000 documents

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions.
  • While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.
  • Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions. Here are the details.

While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.

As part of the proceedings, Epic had submitted 16 categories of documents it wanted Apple to produce (including “internal analyses of the financial or business impact” of its proposed commissions and “communications relating to any strategies to dissuade developers from offering link-outs”), along with a list of current and former Apple employees whose records should be searched.

Apple agreed to use Epic’s proposed search terms and include all employees, and began producing documents it determined were responsive to Epic’s requests.

Epic, however, noted last Friday that Apple was improperly withholding more than 122,000 documents matching those search terms from the records of the seven initial employees, and asked the court to order Apple to produce all matching non-privileged documents, regardless of its relevance assessments.

Which brings us to Apple’s newest filing.

In its filing, Apple argues that contrary to Epic’s claim that its proposed search terms were “tailored” to the proceedings over link-out fees, they were actually “overbroad,” capturing large numbers of unrelated documents.

For instance, Apple notes that while intended to identify documents related to its proposed commission rates, Epic’s “commission*” search term also “captures documents that refer to government and private commissions, as well as documents hitting on the totally irrelevant term ‘commissioner,’ such as documents discussing the NFL Commissioner.”.

“[…] the use of a wildcard in a search string is designated by the asterisk symbol, which means that the search string will hit on any term that includes the prefix before the asterisk.

In the same vein, Apple notes that “Epic’s use of ‘fee*’ in its search strings related to litigation and Apple’s link-out-related projects pulled in documents containing words like ‘feel,’ ‘feed,’ ‘feedback,’ ‘feet,’ and ‘feeble’ without the word ‘fee’ or ‘fees’ appearing at all.”.

Apple’s overall argument is that these unrelated matches account for the vast majority of documents identified by Epic’s searches, and it cites legal precedent to argue that it should only be required to produce documents responsive to Epic’s requests, rather than every document matching the agreed-upon search terms:.

In fact, at least 95% of the Initial Custodian Document Population hit on generic terms like these and did not include any reference to the term “link-out” or its variations, despite that concept being central to the Proffer and related discovery. These sweeping terms do not just increase the total volume of the Initial Custodian Document Population, they also captured highly sensitive and irrelevant documents, such as Apple employees’ personal tax or financial records, medical records, documents discussing unannounced products, documents containing passwords, investor-relations materials, and privileged or protected legal communications.

According to recent reports, the law is clear: parties are only required to produce responsive documents, not every document returned by a search string. […] (“The Court will not compel defendants to produce any document simply because it contains a search term whether or not it is responsive to the discovery request.”). Epic has not shown, and cannot show, why the regular discovery process should be disrupted here. Speculation based on hit counts, particularly where the producing party can explain low responsiveness rates, does not justify the extraordinary and unprecedented remedy Epic seeks.

Apple goes on to argue that complying with Epic’s demands would require extensive additional work, including reviewing documents for privileged or sensitive information and redacting protected material, making it impossible to meet Epic’s proposed December 2 deadline.

Finally, Apple asks the court to reject Epic’s motion but proposes that, should the court decide that some intervention is warranted, a randomized, statistically significant sample of the documents it deems nonresponsive be submitted to a Special Master for independent review, rather than producing all of them to Epic directly.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We don't know about you, but with the chaos of the holidays coming up, the last thing we want is to waste precious brain cells trying to decide what to watch next. That's where Tom's Guide comes in: We do the work of regularly sifting through the best streaming services and their seemingly endless options of fresh movies and television indicates, and compile an easy, breezy TV guide of what exactly you should be clicking "Play" on a given weekend.

And this weekend is no exception: We've sorted through what's recently arrived on Netflix, HBO Max, Paramount Plus, and more and narrowed things down to a trio of great watches, one for each night of your weekend.

On Friday evening, you can hang out with "The Altruists"; the Netflix true-crime drama centers on the biggest crypto fraud in history. Consider Saturday a pseudo date night with one of the world's most legendary chefs, with the HBO Max premiere of the Anthony Bourdain biopic, "Tony." And a lazy Sunday sounds like the perfect day to catch up with the ladies of "Yellowjackets," as the survival thriller kicks off its fourth and final season this week.

Industry observers note that that's a solid weekend of streaming sorted, no? All you have to do is grab some snacks and the remote.

If you love tech-world dramas like "The Dropout," "The Audacity" and "Super Pumped: The Battle for Uber," you'll likely enjoy "The Altruists," a true-crime saga centered on the whirlwind rise and catastrophic collapse of the multi-billion-dollar crypto exchange FTX, which premiered on Netflix on Thursday, November 19.

Starring Anthony Boyle as FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried and three-time Emmy winner Julia Garner as Caroline Ellison—the CEO of FTX's sister hedge fund Alameda Research and Sam's on-and-off-again girlfriend—the eight-part limited series follows the couple's transformation from ambitious young idealists trying to revolutionize the finance world to culprits in an $8 billion scheme that upended the entire crypto market.

The stacked ensemble cast includes Alex Lawther, Karan Soni, Matt Rife, Madison Hu, Paul Reiser, Jennifer Grey, Robin Weigert and "Heated Rivalry" star Hudson Williams.

Stream "The Altruists" on Netflix now.

If you don't know him for his cooking, then you do for his cool: The late, great Anthony Bourdain was one of the most singular figures to come out of the culinary world, so it's no surprise that he'd be the subject of a high-profile bio-drama.

Industry observers note that but instead of charting Bourdain's days as a hotshot chef in top New York kitchens, this Matt Johnson-directed biopic takes it back to the toque's beginnings as an impulsive 19-year-old (played by "The Holdovers" standout Dominic Sessa) working a summer dishwasher job at a local restaurant in 1970s Provincetown, Massachusetts. Under the tutelage of Chef José Vatel (Antonio Banderas) and the gritty restaurant crew, Tony B. gets his first real taste of the chaos and triumphs of a professional kitchen.

The A24 flick—which also stars Emilia Jones, Leo Woodall, Stavros Halkias, and real-life chef icon Eric Ripert—will make its subscription streaming debut on HBO Max on Saturday, November 20.

In a recent development, the final chapter of "Yellowjackets" is finally here, with the survival drama's fourth season premiering on Paramount+ on Friday, November 20. But if you, like yours truly, are a bit behind on the psychological thriller, a long Sunday catching up with the unhinged antics of Shauna (played by Sophie Nélisse in the past and Melanie Lynskey in the present), Taissa (Jasmin Savoy Brown and Tawny Cypress), Misty (Samantha Hanratty and Christina Ricci) and the rest of the gang sounds like a day well spent.

In a recent development, if you're not familiar, "Yellowjackets" follows a 1996 high school girls' soccer team in the aftermath of a plane crash, which leaves them stranded deep in the remote Canadian wilderness. Their fight for survival descends into a psychological nightmare as the girls begin dabbling in ritualized cannibalism, group hunts, and other cultish mysticism. In a parallel timeline set in the present day, the adult survivors must reckon with those dark secrets and long-held regrets 25 years later.

Stream "Yellowjackets" on Paramount+ now.

#51160. UK can’t keep its Apple encryption order secret, tribunal rules

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (547 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thenextweb ↗ Open Full Page

UK can’t keep its Apple encryption order secret, tribunal rules

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (547 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the UK government can no longer keep its Apple encryption order secret, a tribunal has ruled.
  • The order is a technical capability notice under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016.
  • “Anyone with even a passing interest in this topic already knows that the respondent has served a technical capability notice on Apple,” the three judges wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the UK government can no longer keep its Apple encryption order secret, a tribunal has ruled. The Home Office had argued that confirming the order would damage national security. The Investigatory Powers Tribunal rejected that claim in a judgment on Thursday.

The order is a technical capability notice under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016. Such notices can require companies to change how their services work so the authorities can get access to data. Until now the Home Office had refused to confirm or deny it had served one on Apple.

“Anyone with even a passing interest in this topic already knows that the respondent has served a technical capability notice on Apple,” the three judges wrote.

The judges mentioned the government had not kept to its own secrecy policy. The Times and the Financial Times had reported that government sources confirmed the order. The tribunal found that those briefings took place, and that ministers, senior officials or special advisers authorised them.

Recent findings suggest that the Home Office said leak investigations had found no source, but it gave the tribunal no details of them. The government had also let Apple brief senior US officials. The judges called that a further clear departure from its policy. They noted that the answer could be found by typing the question into Google’s chatbot.

Recent findings suggest that the ruling does not make the order’s content public. The judges agreed that publishing all the material would damage national security. But that does not mean every detail must stay secret, they mentioned. The tribunal will decide that question later.

It has been revealed that the parties expect a full hearing in the first half of 2027. Much of it can now take place in public, the judges said. Apple has five grounds of challenge. The tribunal can decide the first two entirely in public. One asks whether the power can reach interception outside the UK. The other asks whether it can be used to regulate the security a company offers its customers.

It has been revealed that apple welcomed the decision as a step in the right direction for public access to the case, Bloomberg reported. Caroline Wilson Palow, legal director of Privacy International, called it a “major victory” for transparency. Privacy International and Liberty brought a separate challenge with two individuals. Liberty called the result a victory for transparency.

The Home Office said the ruling was procedural. Apple has helped police and intelligence agencies for years, and the notice simply requires that it keeps the ability to do so, it said in a statement published by The Register.

“Decisions affecting the safety of the British public must be made by democratically elected governments and independent judges, not in the boardrooms of technology companies,” a government spokesperson said.

Apple filed its second claim in July, after the tribunal dismissed its first. In February 2025 it withdrew Advanced Data Protection for UK owners. The feature extends end-to-end encryption to iCloud backups and more. Meta, TikTok and X also challenged UK data demands this autumn, from Ofcom, and reportedly lost.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pavel Durov speaks at TechCrunch Disrupt Europe in Berlin in October 2013.
  • Telegram CEO Pavel Durov mocked Apple’s iPhone Duo on X, calling it “both too major and too small“, while announcing that Telegram now supports the foldable.
  • Telegram has adapted its app for Apple’s first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, and its CEO used the moment to mock the device.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pavel Durov speaks at TechCrunch Disrupt Europe in Berlin in October 2013.

Telegram CEO Pavel Durov mocked Apple’s iPhone Duo on X, calling it “both too major and too small“, while announcing that Telegram now supports the foldable. The app switches to a two-column layout when the phone is opened.

Telegram has adapted its app for Apple’s first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, and its CEO used the moment to mock the device. “Apple finally made a phone that’s both too big and too small,” Pavel Durov wrote on X on Thursday.

According to recent reports, “It folds in half. Just like your enthusiasm,” he added.

Durov said Telegram still looked “incredible at both wrong sizes,” and joked that the manufacturer does “a lot of charity work.” He shared a short video of the app running on the foldable.

It has been revealed that when the phone is closed, Telegram looks like its usual iPhone version, Brazilian Apple site MacMagazine reported. Opened, it switches to a two-column layout like the iPad app, with chats on one side and the conversation on the other.

The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 and has a 5.4-inch outer screen and a 7.6-inch inner one. It sold out in minutes when preorders opened in October.

Reviewers praised the hinge but noted that many apps still needed updates for the bigger screen. Instagram chief Adam Mosseri mentioned this week that designing for the Duo will be hard.

In a recent development, durov has clashed with Apple before. In August, Apple briefly pulled Telegram from the App Store over a content violation. Durov mentioned extortionists had found a way “to manipulate [Apple] into overreacting.”.

Breaking: Segway E3 Go review: A solid midrange scooter

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Segway E3 Go is a comfortable scooter with front suspension, but it's outshone by the E3 Pro, which can be had for just $50 more, as well as the Apollo Dash, which has a rougher ride, but is better on hills.
  • Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you.
  • Industry observers note that sometimes, you don’t need a monster of an electric scooter to get where you need to go.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Segway E3 Go is a comfortable scooter with front suspension, but it's outshone by the E3 Pro, which can be had for just $50 more, as well as the Apollo Dash, which has a rougher ride, but is better on hills.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Industry observers note that sometimes, you don’t need a monster of an electric scooter to get where you need to go. The Segway E3 Go is made for those with more modest demands for their commute; priced at $649 — but often on sale for less — it also places a more modest demand on your wallet.

I rode the Segway E3 Go for a couple of weeks to get a feel for this mid-range commuter scooter, and to see how it compared to some of the best electric scooters I’ve tested over the years.

According to recent reports, the Segway E3 Go came out in 2026, and retails for $649, though you can often find it on sale for less than $500. For example, for Black Friday, it's discounted to $449 right now.

Segway has put a lot of thought into the feel of its scooters; in recent years, it’s started bending its handlebars slightly back, like on a bike, which gave me a bit more control while I was out and about.

The E3 Go’s deck is also fairly spacious; unless you have gigantic feet, you should have no trouble positioning yourself on the scooter.

I’m also a fan of the E3 Go’s folding mechanism; there’s a small tab at the base of the downtube, which you simply press with your foot to unlock the front half of the scooter and fold it down.

However, you’ll still need a bit of strength to carry it around, as the E3 Go weighs a meaty 46 pounds. The E3 Pro, which has dual suspension and a longer range, is actually six pounds lighter.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

While it lacks the full suspension of its more expensive siblings like the E3 Pro, the Go still has a front suspension. It made for a much smoother ride when going over potholes and other bumps when compared with scooters that lacked such amenities.

Sources indicate that built into the handlebars of the E3 Go are turn signals, which you activate using a thumb switch on the left handlebar; I’ve loved this addition to all electric scooters I’ve tested. I just wish the E3 Go had rear turn signals, like the Segway Max G3 Plus, as it’s hard for cars behind you to see the handlebar signals. I also wish that the E3 Go’s headlight were slightly bigger, and that you could adjust its angle.

Sources indicate that like most of Segway’s scooters, the E3 Go has Apple FindMy, so you can track it if it goes missing. You should always use a lock, but it’s an extra bit of protection.

The 400W motor in the E3 Go proved good, but not great, at climbing hills. On a moderate 5% grade, the scooter slowed to around 10 MPH, which is respectable given its price; however, on a steeper hill with a 6.9% grade — which gets as steep as 10.8% — the E3 Go barely made it to the top, where the similarly-priced Apollo Dash made it up without issue. To be fair, Segway says that the E3 Go is rated to a max grade of 9% (18º slope).

Segway advertises the E3 Go as having a max range of 25 miles; if you set the scooter to its highest performance setting, that estimate drops to just 11.2 miles. I took the E3 Go out for a 5.5-mile ride, and at its conclusion it had 32% battery life remaining, which would mean I would have made it to a little over 8 miles before the battery was completely drained. Of course, your mileage will literally vary based on your weight and the type of riding you do.

Sources indicate that the Segway E3 Go is a good, capable scooter for the price. It should be especially useful in flatter urban areas, and will suit commuters well, so long as you don’t have any major hills to climb. If you have steeper terrain, I would recommend the Apollo Dash; while its ergonomics aren’t as good, it has more power than the Segway, and costs about the same, with many other similar features.

In a recent development, if you can spring for the extra $50, the Segway E3 Pro has dual suspension and a longer range than the E3 Go, and is just as comfortable to ride. Either way, if you have to contend with a lot of potholes, the Segway and its suspension is worth a second look.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

This Note-Taking Pebble Ring Is so Simple, and I Love It

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (902 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos.
  • It has been revealed that in this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity.
  • To buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos. That seems like it would be underwhelming, and the idea was ridiculed by some of Pebble’s fans when the product was first announced. But I’ve been wearing it for a few weeks, and folks: I love it.

It has been revealed that in this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity. This is a ring with no heart rate sensors or even charging pins, just a microphone, a button to activate it, and a light to let you know that it’s working. The audio is processed on your device; no need to send anything to the cloud.

To buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone. I use an iPhone rather than an Android, which means I can’t use certain features like setting timed reminders or connecting to Beeper, but it’s still an incredibly useful little device. The Index has no charger, since it uses a disposable battery that Pebble estimates will last about two years.

The simplest way to use the Index is to wear it on your index finger (hence the name, get it?) and press the button with your thumb. Speak a quick note while holding the button in, and the ring will flash to let you know it got the message. A moment later, you’ll get a notification saying that it added (whatever you said) to your “Notes to self” note.

It has been revealed that to take this further, you can create different notes and ask the ring to add what you say to a specific note. You can also double-click the button to ask a question. The answer will appear in the notification you get on your phone or watch a moment later. (The ring does not speak to you.).

In a recent development, all the notes you leave yourself appear as plain text in the Pebble app, fully editable. If you tap on each one, you can see a timestamp from when you left the note, and you can replay the voice recording if the transcription doesn’t make sense. (Why is there a “pencil sharp pepper” on my packing list? Ohh, that’s a pencil sharpener.) You can also add notes by typing them, which I find useful when starting a to-do list or a packing list.

Sources indicate that it’s incredible how useful a simple timestamped note can be. I used to do something similar with my “notes to self” chat in Signal, but the Index makes it even easier since I won’t get distracted by opening my phone. For example, I make a note on the Index whenever I take a medication, so that tomorrow morning I will be able to check whether I already took, say, a long-acting allergy pill. (You do not want to accidentally double up on those.).

Sources indicate that there’s one thing that, for years, I wished for a simple tool to help me do. It’s trivial, which makes it extra frustrating that I have not been able to find a good solution. I would simply like to note when I leave for a road trip, and when I start and end each stop. This way I can tell how long the driving took as a portion of the whole trip, and how long my stops tend to be so I can blueprint them better next time.

You’d think this would be easy, but every existing tool drove me nuts in a different way. Stopwatches only store a single number, so I can’t break down how long each stop was—and if I miss a button press, I’m screwed. Sending myself a Signal text is probably my best option, but if I’ve just parked my car after three hours of driving, the second I pick up my phone I’m going to see all the notifications that arrived while I was on the road, and I’ll forget to actually send that text.

According to recent reports, but this is exactly what the Index does well. I don’t even need to open my phone or look at my watch. Pressing the button with my thumb means I can do this one-handed without having a microphone always listening. (It’s also a great way to jot down the random things I think of while driving.).

Recent findings suggest that the Index worked perfectly for my travel log, and I even used it for a workout after I got to my hotel room that night. I’d do 10 pushups, then tell the ring “add 10 pushups to my workout.” I’d do 20 crunches, and add that as well. I left the workout note open on my phone and could glance over and see what I had already done, since my messages got added to the note as I went.

Industry observers note that I didn’t need a workout app for any of this, or a special-purpose travel app. I can just leave myself a dang note, and the note-taking app can remember when I left the note and, if I choose, play back exactly how I mentioned it. It’s gloriously simple. Good job, Pebble.
